pronunciation.approximation: 'CHEEL-song' — The first consonant is aspirated; the second syllable ends in a velar nasal. The name refers to the seven stars of the Northern Dipper.

kin.label: Chinese 七星
kin.form: qīxīng, from Middle Chinese tshit-sjeng (Pulleyblank, Lexicon of Reconstructed Pronunciation in Early Middle Chinese) — the Sino-Korean name borrows the Chinese name of the Northern Dipper wholesale.

kin.label: Japanese 七星
kin.form: Shichisei — the same characters read in Japanese; the seven stars are the Northern Dipper, Hokuto, in Japanese star lore.

kin.label: Korean
kin.form: 칠성 Chilseong; the spirit form 칠성신 Chilseongsin — the standard Hangul forms (Revised Romanization of Korean, National Institute of the Korean Language).

pronunciation.note: Chilsong is Tier 2: the romanised name is plain Latin with no diacritic to preserve. The distinctive forms live in Hangul (칠성) and Hanja (七星); the IPA above reflects the Korean reading of the Hangul form. The aspirated first consonant and velar-nasal close are ordinary Korean phonology, not marks of the sacred.

domains.title: Chilsong, the Seven Stars
domains.subtitle: celestial spirits of the Big Dipper, longevity, and fate
domains.lead: Chilsong — 七星, “seven stars” — is the Korean name of the Big Dipper, worshipped as a family of celestial spirits, Chilseongsin, who keep the register of human life and death. Buddhist rites, Joseon court protocol, and village shamanic custom all address the same seven lights circling the pole above the northern sky.

cards.name: Seven Star Spirit
cards.desc: Chilseongsin are the seven star gods as a single household of spirits — patrons of the newborn, the sick, and the dying in Korean folk religion.

cards.name: Northern Dipper
cards.desc: The Dipper circles the pole without setting; Korean star lore reads its circuit as the turning wheel of each person's allotted span of days.

cards.name: Longevity
cards.desc: Offerings to the seven stars petition for added years: court protocols and village rites alike ask the Dipper to extend a life nearing its term.

cards.name: Buddhist Chilseong
cards.desc: Korean monasteries built Chilsong-gak shrine halls where monks chant for the stars' protection — stellar spirits seated within a Buddhist pantheon.

symbols.name: Big Dipper
symbols.meaning: The seven stars of handle and bowl that never set — the visible office of the star spirits.

symbols.name: Peach of immortality
symbols.meaning: The fruit of long life in East Asian lore, offered to the star spirits in longevity rites.

symbols.name: Tortoise and snake
symbols.meaning: The Dark Warrior Hyeonmu (Chinese Xuanwu) of the northern quarter, directional counterpart of the Dipper's sky-sector.

symbols.name: Seven lamps or candles
symbols.meaning: Ritual lights set out in the Dipper's pattern for the Chilseong rite — the constellation reassembled on earth.

mythology.lead: No epic tells Chilsong's story; the sources are court protocol, monastic liturgy, and village custom, and on one point they agree — the seven lights of the northern sky keep each person's days. What follows is attested in Joseon-era records, Buddhist ritual, and the folklore collections of the National Folk Museum of Korea. Where the traditions diverge, the divergence is itself instructive.

myths.title: The Seven Lights Who Keep the Days
myths.text: In Korean folk religion, as recorded in the collections of the National Folk Museum of Korea, the seven stars of the Big Dipper are not lights but officials: Chilseongsin, the star spirits, who keep the register of every life beneath the northern sky. When a child is born, the days are written in the Dipper's book; when a life nears its term, the household may appeal. The appeal has a fixed liturgy — the shaman's Chilseong-gut, in which the seven spirits are invoked and petitioned with rice, clean cloth, and lamps set out in the pattern of the stars. The rite does not beg an unknowable heaven; it negotiates with a bureaucracy whose office is overhead, whose hours are marked by the Dipper's slow circuit of the pole. The constellation is imagined less as distant fire than as a court of record — a sky that keeps books on every life below it, and can, on the strength of a good petition, amend them.

myths.title: The Ch'ilseongnan, Averting the Stars' Calamity
myths.text: When crisis struck the Joseon dynasty — invasion, epidemic, a comet over the palace — the court did not appeal to heaven in the abstract; it addressed the seven stars by name. The uigwe, the royal protocols of the Joseon court, prescribe the Ch'ilseongnan (七星難), the rite for averting the calamity of the seven stars, performed by the king and his ministers in the palace precinct to turn aside the disasters the Dipper was believed capable of sending upon the state. Buddhist monks chanted stellar liturgy while officials processed with offerings — a distinctly Korean arrangement in which the stars received the honors of temple and throne in a single ceremony. Kim Seong Uk's study of these rites shows how thoroughly stellar worship was woven into Joseon state ideology: the dynasty treated the Big Dipper as a power whose goodwill was a matter of national security, to be courted with the same protocol it offered its own ancestors.

myths.title: The Three Sevens of the Newborn
myths.text: Korean birth custom preserves the Dipper's jurisdiction over the cradle. For twenty-one days after a birth — the samchil, the “three sevens” — mother and child were secluded, and folklore collections from every province record the reason: the seven star spirits visit the house on the seventh, fourteenth, and twenty-first nights to inspect the newborn and confirm the span of days allotted to it. A mother who crossed the threshold or handled a blade risked drawing the stars' attention to the child's account. On the twenty-first day the seclusion ended with rice cakes shared among the neighbors — the household re-entering the world only after the last audit. Grayson notes that such customs made the stars' book-keeping tangible at the most vulnerable threshold of life: the Dipper's first inscription of a person happens not at death but at the cradle, and for three weeks the whole village behaves as though the sky were watching.

myths.title: The Stars Receive a Hall
myths.text: Buddhism, arriving in Korea, did not abolish the star spirits — it gave them architecture. Korean monasteries built Chilsong-gak, “halls of the seven stars,” set often apart from the main precinct, where monks chant petitions for longevity and protection; the Chilsong-jae rite seats the seven stars within the Buddhist cosmos as benevolent deities alongside the guardians of the directions. In the shaman's gut the same spirits descend to the drum — the Chilseong-gut is among the most musically elaborate of Korean shamanic rites. The sources preserve no epic of the seven stars, and they disagree on details of office and identity; but on the practice all three traditions — Buddhist, courtly, and shamanic — concur. The Dipper belongs to everyone at once, which is the surest sign of how deeply it belongs: a name so common that temple, palace, and village hut each keep a copy.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 七 (chil, "seven") and 星 (song, "star"). Read 칠성 in Korean, it refers to the seven stars of the Big Dipper and the spirits associated with them.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Chilsong, the Hangul form is 칠성 and the Hanja form is 七星. Hangul ‘칠성’ and Hanja ‘七星’; the figure is also known as Chilseongsin in shamanic and Buddhist contexts. The ASCII form chilsong is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Chilsong is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Chilsong is a layered figure, and its layers can still be counted. The astronomical core is pan-East Asian: the seven stars of the Northern Dipper circle the pole without setting, and across China, Korea, and Japan they were read as the pivot around which the sky's administration turned. The Sinitic complex that accompanied the characters 七星 made the Dipper the arbiter of lifespan, and Korean religion received both together. In Korea the figure was then shaped by Buddhist star liturgy — temples built Chilsong-gak halls and chanted for the stars — by Joseon court protocol, which treated their goodwill as a matter of state, and by village shamanism, whose Chilseong-gut has a distinctive musical and choreographic idiom of its own. The Dark Warrior Hyeonmu (Chinese Xuanwu, the tortoise entwined with a snake) guards the same northern quarter as the Dipper's directional counterpart. The borrowing is real; but the gut that sings to the seven stars is Korean in accent, and that is the layer that has kept the figure alive.
lore.culturalLegacy: Chilsong's presence in Korean life is practical before it is artistic. Temples still maintain their Chilsong-gak halls and receive petitions for longevity; shamanic paintings of Chilseongsin hang in museum collections — the National Folk Museum of Korea and Seoul's Gahoe Museum hold fine examples of the stern star-sovereign in official robes — and the figure remains one of the most commonly invoked protective deities in Korean Buddhism. The seven-star motif guards talismans, funeral garments, and the corners of traditional house plans. The Dipper also taught Korea its way around the night: it is the first asterism children learn, the pointer to the pole star, and it recurs in astronomy classes, games, and film as shorthand for fate itself. To grow up Korean is to know, almost without being told, which seven stars decide.
lore.extendedMeditation: A name like Chilsong looks like a description, but it hides a revolution. To name the seven stars is to move them from scenery to staff — from lights overhead to officials on duty, keeping the one ledger no household can keep for itself: the count of its days. Every tradition that adopted the Dipper accepted that implication. The Buddhist hall, the palace protocol, and the village gut disagree about ritual detail, but all three proceed from the same astonishing premise: that the sky keeps books, and that books can be petitioned. What the restoration Chilsong commemorates is therefore not a star pattern anyone can see, but an institution — perhaps the oldest continuously maintained bureaucracy in Korean religious life, headquartered seven lights above the pole, still accepting appeals. The ASCII form loses nothing visible, no accent and no exotic letter, and exactly in losing nothing it loses everything: the recognition that this is a proper name, a title of office, the signature on the world's oldest ongoing case file.

lore.archaeology: The material record of Chilsong worship is recent but rich. The seven stars stand at the northern crown of the Cheonsang Yeolcha Bunyajido, the great Korean star chart first engraved on stone in 1395 and recut in 1687 — the surviving copy is National Treasure of Korea no. 228, its three thousand stars centered on the circumpolar region the Dipper governs. The Joseon court's own liturgies survive on paper: the uigwe protocols for the Ch'ilseongnan rite, including the Oegyujanggak set returned from France in 2011 and now held by the National Palace Museum of Korea. And the shamanic layer has its own artifacts: paintings of Chilseongsin in official robes, holding the tablets of life and death, are preserved in the collections of the National Folk Museum of Korea and the Gahoe Museum, Seoul.
